unit.unitOverview: Unit 5 turns you into a writer of instructions. You will take apart a Somali recipe for bariis to see how a title, a materials list, numbered steps and tips work together, and you will learn the zero conditional, the pattern that explains what happens every single time. Alongside the recipe you will read “The Memory Wall”, a story about a class who learn to communicate what matters to them. By the end you will have planned, drafted, tested and revised your own set of instructions that somebody else can genuinely follow.
unit.learningPath: Start with the Overview and the four vocabulary groups. Read “What Makes Instructions Work” and the bariis recipe, then answer the comprehension questions. Work through the six grammar lessons on the zero conditional, imperative verbs, time connectives and prepositions of position. Read “The Memory Wall” in three parts and complete the activities. Practise the four speaking tasks, then plan, draft and revise your procedure across the six writing tasks. Finish with the checkpoint quiz, the self-assessment and the unit portfolio.

readings.title: What Makes Instructions Work
readings.passageScript:
Instructions surround you. A recipe, a board game leaflet and a science experiment are all procedural texts. Each one exists so that a reader can do the job successfully the very first time.
Every strong set of instructions shares the same five parts. The title tells the reader exactly what they are about to make or do. The opening paragraph explains why the task is worth doing and what the reader should expect. The materials list gathers everything needed before the work begins. The numbered steps put the actions in the only order that works. The tips section warns the reader about the mistakes other people have already made.
Two kinds of words do most of the work. Imperative verbs, such as rinse, place, stir and measure, open a step and tell the reader exactly what to do. Time connectives, such as first, next, then, after that, while and finally, show where one step ends and the next begins.
Writers of instructions also use the zero conditional to explain cause and effect. If you lift the lid too early, the steam escapes. Sentences like that turn a bare order into a reason the reader can trust.
The best test of any set of instructions is simple. Hand them to somebody who has never done the task, then watch closely. Every place where that reader pauses is a place where your writing still needs to be clearer.

readings.title: How to Make Bariis: Spiced Rice
readings.setting: Home kitchen in an East African family
readings.passageScript:
Bariis is one of the best-loved dishes in Somali cooking. It is a fragrant, golden rice, seasoned with a blend of warm spices and usually served beside meat, vegetables or sliced banana. Families across East Africa have cooked bariis for many generations, and the recipe has passed from grandmothers to mothers to daughters. Follow the steps below and you can make it yourself, even if this is your first time in the kitchen.
What you will need
Gather everything before you light the stove. Cooks call this preparation mise en place, which is French for putting everything in its place.
2 cups of basmati rice and 3 cups of water
3 tablespoons of vegetable oil or ghee
1 small onion, finely chopped, and 2 cloves of garlic, crushed
1 teaspoon of cumin and 1 teaspoon of cardamom
Half a teaspoon of turmeric, which gives the rice its golden colour
Half a teaspoon of cinnamon and 1 teaspoon of salt
A medium cooking pot with a tight lid, a wooden spoon and a sieve
Steps
1. Rinse the rice. Tip the rice into the sieve and hold it under cold running water, swirling it gently with your fingers until the water runs clear. If you rinse the extra starch away, the grains cook separately instead of sticking together.
2. Soak the rice. Move the rinsed rice into a bowl, cover it with cold water and leave it for at least fifteen minutes. Soaking softens the grains so that they cook evenly and do not break apart.
3. Cook the onion. Place the pot on a medium heat, add the oil and, when it is hot, add the chopped onion. Stir for three or four minutes until the onion turns soft and golden. If the onion burns, the whole dish tastes bitter.
4. Add the garlic and spices. Next, stir in the crushed garlic for thirty seconds, then add the cumin, cardamom, turmeric, cinnamon and salt. Stir for one minute so that the spices combine with the oil and release their flavour.
5. Coat the rice. Drain the soaked rice, add it to the pot and stir gently for two minutes until every grain is coated. This step lets each grain absorb the spices before any water goes in.
6. Pour in the water. Carefully add the three cups of water, stir once so that the rice sits evenly across the base, then raise the heat until the water boils.
7. Cover and simmer. As soon as the water boils, lower the heat as far as it will go and fit the lid tightly. Leave the rice for eighteen to twenty minutes. If you lift the lid, the steam escapes and the rice stays hard.
8. Rest and fluff. Turn off the heat, but leave the lid on for five more minutes. Finally, lift the lid and separate the grains with a fork. Your bariis is ready to serve.
Tips
Ghee gives a richer flavour than oil if you have it.
One whole clove or a small stick of cinnamon adds extra aroma.
Bariis is traditionally served on one large plate, with the rice in the centre and the meat or vegetables arranged around it.
Always ask an adult for help with the stove and with hot pots.
If the rice sticks to the base of the pot, the heat was too high, so lower it further next time.

readings.title: The Memory Wall, part 1
readings.setting: Umoja Primary School library and classroom
readings.passageScript:
At Umoja Primary School, the Year 5 class came back from lunch buzzing with energy. Something near the library was different. A long strip of brown paper had been pinned across the wall, and above it somebody had written six words: “If you remember it, write it.”
Underneath, short passages had already appeared, each in a different pupil's handwriting. One read, “The time I got lost and was found again at school.” Another read, “When my cousin taught me how to ride a bike.”
“Who made this?” asked Leo, scratching his head.
“I have no idea,” said Nora, standing at the fringe of the growing crowd. “But it is interesting.”
Their teacher, Teacher Yasmin, came in and smiled. “This is our Memory Wall. Every one of you will add a story this week.”
“What kind of story?” asked Leo.
“Anything that made you think, feel or learn,” she said. “Your memories will help us understand our own emotions, and our generation's voice.”
Leo looked nervous. “What if I cannot remember anything exciting?”
“If you combine honesty with feeling, it is worth reading,” Teacher Yasmin said. “Start with a moment that surprised you or changed the way you think.”
Nora whispered, “That sounds hard. I would rather draw.”
“Then combine pictures and words,” said Teacher Yasmin. “Draw and write. Communicate in your own way.”
That evening, Leo sat at his desk and thought about his grandfather. The memory arrived in small pieces, in the same way his grandfather's voice used to fade as he fell asleep in the middle of a story.
Leo began to write. “One evening, Grandpa told me about a boy who was once a slave. He could not read, but he remembered every word he heard. Grandpa said that the boy's memory was a gift, and that mine was a gift too.”
He stopped and read the lines again. Was that memory good enough?

readings.title: The Memory Wall, part 2
readings.setting: Umoja Primary School library and classroom
readings.passageScript:
Then Leo added one more line. “I did not move or inhale too loudly. I simply kept listening until the words stayed with me.”
The next day, Teacher Yasmin led a class discussion. “If you feel something important, write it down,” she said. “If we combine our stories and our voices, we grow stronger.”
Nora raised her hand. “I would like to include a quote from my grandmother.”
“What is the quote?” Teacher Yasmin asked.
Nora smiled. “She always said, ‘You do not need permission to shine.’”
“That is beautiful,” the teacher replied. “We should emphasise voices like that one.”
“Some people might assume that stories are only about big events,” said Amal.
“But if you navigate a difficult feeling, that is a big event,” Teacher Yasmin said.
After lunch, the class took turns adding to the wall. A few pupils paused or hesitated at the last moment.
“Do not hesitate, Leo,” said Nora. “Yours is good. It is honest.” Her steady words seemed to encourage him.
He smiled, walked over and pasted his passage beside Nora's drawing.
Amal pointed at it. “Did your grandfather really say that?”
“He did,” Leo replied.
“That was wise,” said Amal. “It made me think about Grandma Hana, who tells stories too.”
That afternoon, Teacher Yasmin held a reflection circle. “What emerged from our stories?” she asked.
“We are not so different,” said Nora. “Everybody has a memory that made them feel frightened, happy or proud.”
Leo added, “If you listen carefully, people say things that stay with you. Even when the words fade, the meaning remains.”
Teacher Yasmin nodded. “That is the power of communication.”

readings.title: The Memory Wall, part 3
readings.setting: Umoja Primary School library and classroom
readings.passageScript:
On Friday, the last day of the Memory Wall, Teacher Yasmin invited a local author to read the pupils' work aloud.
He read Nora's drawing-story and Leo's memory. “I am touched,” he said. “These words are better than many books I have read.” He paused. “Who wrote this one, about the boy who remembered everything he heard?”
Leo raised his hand. “It is mine.”
“Did you know that generations ago, stories travelled only by memory? You have honoured that tradition.”
Leo felt his heart race, and this time it was not fear. It was pride.
At home that night, Leo's younger brother asked, “What is a slave?”
Leo thought carefully before he answered. “A slave is somebody who was forced to work and was not allowed any freedom. But those people still had their own thoughts, their own stories and their own hope.”
“Like Grandpa's story?”
“Yes,” said Leo, smiling. “And now I have written it down, so it will not be forgotten.”
The following week, the Memory Wall came down, but nobody threw it away. Instead, the class turned it into a book.
“Your work will be shared with next year's pupils,” said Teacher Yasmin. “You have built something real.”
“I did not expect that,” said Nora.
“You believed in one another,” said Teacher Yasmin. “You united, didn't you?”
“Definitely,” said Leo. “We did not exaggerate anything. We simply told the truth.”

comprehension.question: In “What Makes Instructions Work”, which five parts does every strong set of instructions share?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They share the title, the opening paragraph, the materials list, the numbered steps and the tips section.
comprehension.explanation: The second paragraph names each part in turn and gives every one of them its own job.

comprehension.question: The text says to hand your instructions to somebody who has never done the task. Why is watching that reader useful?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Every place where the reader pauses shows the writer exactly which step is not yet clear enough.
comprehension.explanation: The final paragraph turns the reader's pauses into a map of the weak steps, so the writer knows what to redraft.

comprehension.question: How long should the rinsed rice soak before it is cooked, and why?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It soaks in cold water for at least fifteen minutes, which softens the grains so they cook evenly.
comprehension.explanation: Step 2 gives both the time and the reason, so a complete answer needs the fifteen minutes and the softening.

comprehension.question: In the bariis recipe, which step comes immediately after the spices have been stirred into the oil?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The drained rice is added to the pot and stirred gently for two minutes until every grain is coated.
comprehension.explanation: Step 4 ends with the spices releasing their flavour, and step 5 coats the rice before any water is poured in.

comprehension.question: Why does the bariis recipe warn you not to lift the lid while the rice is simmering?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Lifting the lid lets the steam escape, and the steam is what cooks the rice, so the grains stay hard.
comprehension.explanation: Step 7 states the cause and effect as a zero conditional, which is why the warning is a fact rather than a guess.

comprehension.question: The bariis recipe gives rinsing a whole numbered step of its own. Why is that worth the space?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Rinsing washes the extra starch away, so the grains cook separately instead of sticking into one lump.
comprehension.explanation: Step 1 explains the purpose, and a reader who skips it gets sticky rice, so the step earns its place.

comprehension.question: What six words had been written above the strip of brown paper on the Memory Wall?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The words were “If you remember it, write it.”
comprehension.explanation: The opening paragraph of part 1 quotes the invitation that started the whole project.

comprehension.question: How does Leo feel when Teacher Yasmin first explains the task, and which line proves it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He feels nervous, and the proof is his question, “What if I cannot remember anything exciting?”
comprehension.explanation: The narrator says Leo looked nervous, and his own question supplies the evidence for that feeling.

comprehension.question: Nora tells Leo not to hesitate at the wall. What does “hesitate” mean at that moment in part 2?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It means he paused before pinning his writing up, because he was unsure whether his memory was good enough.
comprehension.explanation: The narrator says a few pupils paused or hesitated, so the surrounding sentence supplies the meaning.

comprehension.question: Why does Teacher Yasmin say that navigating a difficult feeling is a big event?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means that working your way through a hard emotion takes real courage, so it deserves a place on the wall.
comprehension.explanation: She answers Amal, who assumed that only large events count, and the reply widens what a memory may be about.

comprehension.question: What happened to the Memory Wall in the week after it came down?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Nobody threw it away; the class turned it into a book to share with next year's pupils.
comprehension.explanation: Part 3 ends with the wall becoming a book, which is why Teacher Yasmin says the class built something real.

comprehension.question: Leo says his heart raced but that the feeling was not fear. What was it, and what caused it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The feeling was pride, caused by the visiting author praising his memory in front of the whole class.
comprehension.explanation: The narrator names the feeling directly, and the praise from the author in the paragraph before is its cause.

grammar.title: What the Zero Conditional Is For
grammar.explanation: The zero conditional describes results that follow every single time. Scientists reach for it to state facts, and instruction writers reach for it to explain what happens when a step is done properly or skipped.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Zero conditional sentences carry no doubt at all: if the condition is met, the result always follows.
Science: If you heat ice, it melts. If the temperature drops below zero, water freezes. If you mix vinegar and bicarbonate of soda, it fizzes.
Everyday life: If the sun sets, it gets dark. If you do not eat, you feel hungry. If it rains, the ground gets wet.
Instructions: If you follow the steps carefully, you get good results. If the jar is not clean, the experiment fails.
Warnings: If you stir the mixture too quickly, it splashes. If you leave bread in the sun, it dries out.
The pattern earns the name zero because there is zero chance of any different outcome.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often reach for the zero conditional to describe one particular afternoon. Kind fix: keep it for what is true every time, and test the sentence by saying every time inside your head.
grammar.memoryTip: Swap the word if for every time. If the sentence still makes sense, it is a zero conditional: every time you heat ice, it melts.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Write ZC beside every sentence that is always true. | If you heat metal, it expands. | If it rains tomorrow, I will take an umbrella. | If it rains, the ground gets wet. | If you study hard, you will pass the exam. | If we leave now, we will arrive on time. | Part B. For each ZC sentence, write one sentence explaining why the result never changes. | Part C. Find two zero conditional sentences in the bariis recipe and copy them out.

Answer key — try every part yourself first, then check.
Part A: Zero conditional — "If you heat metal, it expands." and "If it rains, the ground gets wet." NOT zero conditional — "If it rains tomorrow, I will take an umbrella.", "If you study hard, you will pass the exam." and "If we leave now, we will arrive on time." (these use will to predict one occasion, not a fact that is always true).
Part B: This asks for your own words, so there is no single fixed answer — check that your sentence explains why the cause always produces the same result every time. Model example: "If you heat metal, it expands, because heat always makes the particles in the metal move further apart."
Part C: Any two of these three sentences from the bariis recipe are zero conditionals: "If you rinse the extra starch away, the grains cook separately instead of sticking together." / "If the onion burns, the whole dish tastes bitter." / "If you lift the lid, the steam escapes and the rice stays hard."

grammar.title: How to Form the Zero Conditional
grammar.explanation: Both halves of a zero conditional sit in the present simple. Nothing in the sentence looks forward, because the result is already a settled fact rather than a prediction.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Pattern: If + subject + present simple verb, subject + present simple verb.
If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.
The if-clause names the condition; the main clause names the result.
Comma rule: when the if-clause comes first, put a comma after it. When the main clause comes first, no comma is needed.
If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
You get purple if you mix red and blue.
The word when replaces if with the same meaning: When you heat water, it boils.
More examples: If you press the button, the light turns on. If you add sugar to tea, it tastes sweet. If you use warm water, the salt dissolves faster. If you drop something, it falls. If you practise every day, you improve.
From “The Memory Wall”: If you combine honesty with feeling, it is worth reading. If we combine our stories and our voices, we grow stronger. If you listen carefully, people say things that stay with you.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: If you drop a glass it breaks. The comma after the if-clause has gone missing. Fix: If you drop a glass, it breaks. Read the line aloud and put the comma where your voice pauses.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture two matching halves: present simple on the left, present simple on the right. An if-clause in front takes the comma; an if-clause behind takes none.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Write the correct present simple form of each verb in brackets. | If you ______ (mix) flour and water, you ______ (make) dough. | If it ______ (rain) heavily, the river ______ (flood). | If you ______ (not sleep) enough, you ______ (feel) tired. | If the alarm ______ (go) off, we ______ (leave) the building. | If you ______ (combine) sugar and butter, the mixture ______ (become) smooth. | If you ______ (not wear) a coat, you ______ (get) cold. | If we ______ (work) together, we ______ (finish) faster. | If you ______ (press) this button, the door ______ (open). | Part B. Match each if-clause to its result, then write the full sentence with the comma in place. | If you water the plants, ... | If you heat ice, ... | If the sun shines, ... | If you mix red and blue, ... | If you read every day, ... | Results: they grow / it melts / the room gets bright / you get purple / your vocabulary improves. | Part C. Rewrite each fact as one zero conditional sentence with the if-clause first. | Water boils at 100 degrees. | Plants die without water. | Metal expands when it gets hot. | People get sunburnt without sunscreen. | Mixing blue and yellow paint produces green paint. | Not brushing your teeth causes cavities. | Leaving milk out of the fridge causes it to go sour. | Part D. Rewrite two of your Part C answers with the main clause first, and delete the comma.

Answer key — try every part yourself first, then check.
Part A: 1. mix, make 2. rains, floods 3. do not sleep (don't sleep), feel 4. goes, leave 5. combine, becomes 6. do not wear (don't wear), get 7. work, finish 8. press, opens.
Part B: If you water the plants, they grow. If you heat ice, it melts. If the sun shines, the room gets bright. If you mix red and blue, you get purple. If you read every day, your vocabulary improves.
Part C: Model rewrites (close variants are fine as long as the if-clause comes first, both halves use present simple, and a comma follows the if-clause): If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils. If plants do not get water, they die. If metal gets hot, it expands. If people do not wear sunscreen, they get sunburnt. If you mix blue and yellow paint, you get green paint. If you do not brush your teeth, you get cavities. If you leave milk out of the fridge, it goes sour.
Part D: Open-ended, since it depends on which two of your Part C sentences you pick — there is no single fixed answer. Model example: "Plants die if they do not get water." and "It boils if you heat water to 100 degrees." (main clause first, no comma).

grammar.title: Zero Conditional or First Conditional?
grammar.explanation: The first conditional predicts one possible future; the zero conditional states a permanent fact. The difference shows itself in the main clause, where the first conditional needs the word will.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Zero conditional: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils. This is true every time.
First conditional: If you heat the water, it will be ready for tea. This is one particular occasion.
Zero: If you drop an egg, it breaks. First: If you drop that egg, it will make a mess on the floor.
Zero: If plants do not get sunlight, they die. First: If we do not water the garden today, the flowers will probably wilt.
Zero: If you mix vinegar and bicarbonate of soda, it fizzes. First: If you try this experiment, you will see something surprising.
Grammar difference: the zero conditional uses the present simple twice, while the first conditional uses the present simple and then will plus the base verb.
Test: ask whether the sentence is always true or true only once. Always true takes two present simple verbs; one future event takes will.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: If you heat ice, it will melt. The word will turns a permanent fact into a prediction. Fix: If you heat ice, it melts. Mistake: If you heated water, it boils. The past tense belongs in neither conditional. Fix: If you heat water, it boils.
grammar.memoryTip: The word will points at one single moment in the future. A fact that never changes has no single moment to point at, so it never needs will.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Each sentence contains one error. Rewrite it correctly and say what was wrong. | If you will add salt to water, it dissolves. | If water freezed, it becomes ice. | If you touched fire it burns you. | If it rain, the roads get slippery. | If plants does not get light, they die. | If you doesn't study, you fails the test. | If you will drop a ball, it bounces. | If you mix red and yellow you get orange. | Part B. Write ZC or FC beside each sentence. | If it rains tomorrow, I will take an umbrella. | If you heat metal, it expands. | If we leave now, we will arrive on time. | If plants do not get water, they die. | If you study hard, you will pass the exam. | Part C. Write five zero conditional sentences of your own, one each about nature, cooking, school, health and daily life.

Part A: 1. Error: will used in a zero conditional. Fix: If you add salt to water, it dissolves. 2. Error: freezed is not a present-simple verb. Fix: If water freezes, it becomes ice. 3. Error: past tense in the if-clause, and a missing comma. Fix: If you touch fire, it burns you. 4. Error: rain should be rains. Fix: If it rains, the roads get slippery. 5. Error: does should be do (plants is plural). Fix: If plants do not get light, they die. 6. Error: doesn't should be don't, and fails should be fail (subject is you). Fix: If you don't study, you fail the test. 7. Error: will used in a zero conditional. Fix: If you drop a ball, it bounces. 8. Error: missing comma after the if-clause. Fix: If you mix red and yellow, you get orange.
Part B: If it rains tomorrow, I will take an umbrella. — FC. If you heat metal, it expands. — ZC. If we leave now, we will arrive on time. — FC. If plants do not get water, they die. — ZC. If you study hard, you will pass the exam. — FC.
Part C: Open-ended, since these are your own sentences — there is no single fixed answer. Model examples, one per topic: Nature — If it does not rain for weeks, the ground cracks. Cooking — If you overcook pasta, it turns soft. School — If you do not do your homework, the teacher notices. Health — If you do not sleep enough, you feel tired. grammar.title: Imperative Verbs: The Command Words of Instructions
grammar.explanation: An imperative verb gives a direct order. Procedural writing leans on it, because every step must tell the reader precisely what to do without wasting a single word.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
An imperative uses the base form of the verb with no subject in front of it: Rinse. Place. Stir. Measure.
In instructions the imperative opens the sentence: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear.
Imperative verbs in “How to Make Bariis”: rinse, place, hold, soak, add, stir, drain, pour, cover, leave, turn, lift, separate, gather, ask.
Negative orders take do not: Do not lift the lid during this time.
The word please softens an order: Please gather everything before you start.
Let us includes the speaker: Let us try the recipe together on Saturday.
An imperative never carries a subject pronoun, so You stir the onion becomes Stir the onion.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: You should probably stir the onion now. The order disappears inside a suggestion. Fix: Stir the onion for three minutes. A reader halfway through a recipe wants the action, not the hedge.
grammar.memoryTip: Cover the first word of any step in the bariis recipe. If the rest still makes sense as an order given to you, the word you covered was an imperative verb.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Find eight imperative verbs in “How to Make Bariis” and copy the step that each one opens. | Part B. Rewrite each sentence as an imperative. | You should wash your hands first. | It is sensible to weigh the flour before you begin. | I want you to close the lid tightly. | Learners must not touch the hot pot. | Part C. Write four steps for tidying your desk, opening every step with a different imperative verb. | Part D. Turn two of your Part C steps into polite orders using please.

Answer key — try every part yourself first, then check.
Part A: Open-ended, since more than eight imperative verbs appear in "How to Make Bariis" (see the rule and examples above for the full list) — any eight are correct. Model answer using eight of them: Rinse — "Rinse the rice." Soak — "Soak the rice." Add — "Add the garlic and spices." Drain — "Drain the soaked rice, add it to the pot and stir gently for two minutes until every grain is coated." Pour — "Pour in the water." Cover — "Cover and simmer." Turn — "Turn off the heat, but leave the lid on for five more minutes." Gather — "Gather everything before you light the stove."
Part B: Wash your hands first. Weigh the flour before you begin. Close the lid tightly. Do not touch the hot pot.
Part C: Open-ended, since these are your own steps — there is no single fixed answer. Model example: "Clear the papers off the desk. Sort the pens into the pot. Wipe the surface with a cloth. Stack the books in the corner."
Part D: Open-ended, since it depends on which two of your Part C steps you pick — there is no single fixed answer. Model example: "Please clear the papers off the desk." / "Please wipe the surface with a cloth."

grammar.title: Time Connectives: Putting the Steps in Order
grammar.explanation: Time connectives are the signposts of a procedure. They tell the reader where one action stops and the next begins, so the order of the steps can never be mistaken.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Openers that start a sequence: first, to begin, before you start.
Middle markers: next, then, after that, once, when, while, as soon as, meanwhile.
Closers: finally, at the end, lastly.
From “How to Make Bariis”: Next, stir in the crushed garlic for thirty seconds. As soon as the water boils, lower the heat. Finally, lift the lid and separate the grains with a fork.
The words while and meanwhile show two actions happening together: While the rice soaks, chop the onion.
A time connective at the front of a sentence is followed by a comma: After that, cover the pot.
Do not open every step with then, because a reader stops noticing a word that never changes.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: Then add the water then cover the pot then wait. The steps blur into one line. Fix: give each step its own sentence and vary the connective. Next, add the water. After that, cover the pot. Finally, wait for twenty minutes.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of a race: one word for the start, several for the middle and one for the finish. First gets you going, next and after that keep you moving, and finally brings you home.
grammar.practice:
Part A. List five time connectives in “How to Make Bariis” and name the step each one introduces. | Part B. Put these steps in the right order and join them with time connectives. | Fold the paper in half. | Gather your paper and scissors. | Cut carefully along the fold. | Decorate both halves. | Part C. Rewrite this instruction so that no connective repeats: Then boil the water, then add the tea, then pour the milk, then serve. | Part D. Write three steps that use while or meanwhile to show two actions happening together.

Answer key — try every part yourself first, then check.
Part A: Model answer (any five connectives from the passage are correct): Next — introduces "stir in the crushed garlic for thirty seconds" (step 4, adding the garlic and spices). then — introduces "add the cumin, cardamom, turmeric, cinnamon and salt" (step 4). when — introduces "add the chopped onion" (step 3, cooking the onion). As soon as — introduces "lower the heat" (step 7, cover and simmer). Finally — introduces "lift the lid and separate the grains with a fork" (step 8, rest and fluff).
Part B: First, gather your paper and scissors. Next, fold the paper in half. After that, cut carefully along the fold. Finally, decorate both halves.
Part C: Model rewrite: "First, boil the water. Next, add the tea. After that, pour the milk. Finally, serve."
Part D: Open-ended, since these are your own steps — there is no single fixed answer. Model example: "While the rice cooks, chop the vegetables. Meanwhile, set the table. While the pot cools down, wash the dishes."

grammar.title: Prepositions of Position and the Shape of a Procedural Text
grammar.explanation: Instructions must say where things go as well as what to do. Prepositions of position pin an object to an exact place, and the layout of the text pins each part of the writing to its own purpose.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Prepositions of position: in, on, under, beside, between, above.
in — inside a space: Place the rice in the sieve.
on — resting on a surface: Place the pot on the stove.
under — below something: Hold the sieve under the running water.
beside — next to: Stand the wooden spoon beside the pot.
between — in the middle of two things: Leave a gap between the plate and the bowl.
above — higher than, without touching: Hang the recipe card above the worktop.
The five parts of a procedural text, in order: title, opening paragraph, materials list, numbered steps, tips.
Each part has one job. The title names the task, the opening explains why it matters, the list gathers what is needed, the steps give the actions in order, and the tips warn about likely mistakes.
Bulleted lists suit materials, because order does not matter. Numbered lists suit steps, because the numbers carry the order.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: Put the spoon in the pot when you mean beside it. The reader drops the spoon into hot oil. Fix: choose the preposition that matches the picture in your head, then read the step back and check the picture again.
grammar.memoryTip: Say the position words while you move a pencil around your desk: in the tray, on the book, under the chair, beside the lamp, between the pens, above the shelf.
grammar.practice:
Part A. Choose in, on, under, beside, between or above for each gap. | The sieve waits ______ the running tap. | The pot sits ______ the stove. | The salt jar stands ______ the pepper jar. | The recipe card is pinned ______ the worktop. | The soaking rice rests ______ the bowl. | The chopping board lies ______ the sink and the stove. | Part B. Label the five parts of “How to Make Bariis” and write one sentence explaining what each part is for. | Part C. Decide whether a bulleted list or a numbered list suits each of these, and give your reason: the materials list, the set of steps, the safety warnings. | Part D. Write three instructions of your own for setting a table, using three different prepositions of position.

Answer key — try every part yourself first, then check.
Part A: The sieve waits under the running tap. The pot sits on the stove. The salt jar stands beside the pepper jar. The recipe card is pinned above the worktop. The soaking rice rests in the bowl. The chopping board lies between the sink and the stove.
Part B: Title — "How to Make Bariis: Spiced Rice": names the task. Opening paragraph — the paragraph about bariis being a loved Somali dish: explains why the dish matters and reassures a first-time cook. Materials list — "What you will need": gathers the ingredients and equipment before cooking starts. Numbered steps — "Steps" 1 to 8: gives the actions in the order they must be done. Tips — the final "Tips" section: warns about likely mistakes and adds extra advice.
Part C: Materials list — bulleted, because the order you gather things in does not matter. Set of steps — numbered, because each step must be done in the right order. Safety warnings — bulleted, because each warning stands on its own and does not depend on the others.
Part D: Open-ended, since these are your own instructions — there is no single fixed answer. Model example: "Put the placemat on the table. Place the napkin beside the plate. Put the fork between the plate and the knife."

speaking.title: Speaking 1: The Instruction Game (Pairs)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work with a partner. One of you is the instructor and the other is the follower.
The instructor chooses a simple task, such as making a paper aeroplane, drawing a particular shape or arranging four objects on a desk. Without showing the follower what the finished result should look like, the instructor gives spoken step-by-step instructions. The follower must listen and carry out each step exactly as it is described. Compare the two results, then swap roles and choose a different task.
Model lines for the instructor: “First, place the sheet of paper in front of you.” “Next, fold it in half from top to bottom.” “After that, press along the fold with your thumb.” “Finally, turn the paper over and repeat the fold.”
Model lines for the follower: “Sorry, could you repeat step two more slowly?” “Do you mean the long edge or the short edge?”
Talk about it afterwards: Were the instructions clear enough? Which imperative verbs and time connectives did the instructor use? What would the instructor change next time? What did the follower do when a step confused them?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play the follower while I give you spoken instructions for folding paper, and tell me exactly where you got stuck.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Explain a Process (Individual Presentation)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose a process that you know really well. It could be washing your hands properly, making a simple snack, braiding hair, looking after a pet or playing your favourite game.
Prepare a spoken presentation of two to three minutes that explains the process step by step to your class or your family. Use clear imperative verbs and time connectives as you speak. Small prompt cards with key words are allowed, but do not read from a full script.
Model opening: “Today I am going to explain how to look after a rabbit. You will need fresh hay, clean water and about ten minutes each morning.”
Model closing: “That is how I look after my rabbit. Is there any step you would like me to explain again?”
Presentation tips: speak slowly enough for your audience to follow each step; use your hands to show the actions; make eye contact; signal every new step with first, next, then or finally.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my two-minute explanation of a process, then tell me which step needed one more sentence.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Interview About Daily Routines (Pairs)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Take turns interviewing your partner about their daily routines. Ask questions such as: How do you get ready for school in the morning? What steps do you follow before bed? How do you organise your school bag?
The person answering should sequence their reply with time connectives. The interviewer should take notes and then summarise the routine back using reporting language.
Model summary: “You said that first you wake up at six o'clock, then you wash your face, and after that you eat breakfast.”
Check together whether the summary is accurate, and add anything that was missed.
Challenge: write a short paragraph summarising your partner's routine. Use at least three time connectives and two zero conditional sentences, for example: “If Nora does not set her alarm, she wakes up late.”
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Interview me about my morning routine, then repeat it back to me using reporting language so I can check it.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Group Instruction Challenge (Small Groups)
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work in groups of three or four. Your group will build one set of spoken instructions that the rest of the class will try to follow.
Choose one of these tasks, or invent your own: tidying a messy classroom in five minutes; setting up a simple obstacle course in the playground; planning a class celebration.
Agree the steps together, then choose one presenter. The presenter speaks the instructions aloud while the class follows them.
Model line for the presenter: “Step three. While two people stack the chairs, the rest of you collect the loose paper from under the desks.”
Afterwards the class gives feedback on three questions: Was every step clear? Was any step missing? What single change would improve the instructions most?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Act as our class while I read out group instructions, and afterwards name the one step that was missing.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Read the Recipe Aloud
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Read three steps of “How to Make Bariis” aloud as though a listener is cooking along with you and cannot see the page.
Slow down on every measurement and every time connective, because those are the words a listener needs most.
Model line: “Step seven. As soon as the water boils — as soon as it boils — lower the heat as far as it will go.”
Record yourself, listen back, and mark one place where you spoke too quickly and one place where a listener might have needed a pause.
Then read the same three steps to a partner who is holding a pencil. If your partner can draw the actions in order, your reading was clear.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen while I read three recipe steps aloud and tell me which measurement I rushed past.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Talk About a Memory
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Prepare a three-minute talk about one memory that made you think, feel or learn, in the way that Leo and Nora did on the Memory Wall.
Structure it in three parts: an opening that sets the scene, two or three connected ideas with real detail, and a closing that says why the memory stayed with you.
Model opening: “The memory I want to share happened at my grandmother's kitchen table, and it lasted about ten minutes.”
Model closing: “Even when the words fade, the meaning remains, and that is why I still think about it.”
Afterwards, take two questions from your listeners and answer each one in a complete sentence. Then say which part of your talk you would change.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my three-minute memory talk and ask me two questions that would make the ending stronger.

writing.title: Writing 1: Plan Your Own Instructions
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose one topic for your own set of instructions, then plan it before you write a single sentence.
Topic choices: how to make a Somali spiced tea called shaah cadays; how to set up an attractive classroom library display; how to prepare for and lead a school assembly.
Complete this planning frame in your book. Title: what will you call your instructions? Purpose: why would somebody need them, and who is your reader? Materials: everything the reader needs before they start. Steps: a short note for each step, between six and ten of them, in order. Tips or warnings: the mistakes your reader is most likely to make. Time connectives: list at least five that you will use.
Do not draft yet. A plan that names the reader and orders the steps saves you rewriting the whole piece later.
writing.modelText:
Title: How to Make Shaah Cadays
Purpose: for a Year 5 pupil who wants to make tea for guests but has never used the stove alone; it is a recipe passed down through generations.
Materials: a small pot, water, black tea leaves, cardamom, cinnamon, sugar, milk, a strainer, cups.
Steps: boil the water; combine the tea and spices in the pot; simmer; add sugar; add milk; strain into cups.
Tips: if you leave the pot alone, the milk boils over; do not hesitate to add a little more sugar for guests.
Time connectives: first, next, after that, meanwhile, finally.
writing.sentenceStarter: My instructions will teach a reader how to...
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Talk the steps through with a partner first, then write each step on a separate strip of paper so you can reorder them.
writing.extension: Add a column to your plan naming the imperative verb that will open each step.

writing.title: Writing 2: Draft the Opening Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Study this model opening, then write your own.
Model: Shaah cadays is a warm, sweet, fragrant tea enjoyed in Somali homes every day. Whether it is served in the morning or in the evening when guests arrive, this spiced tea brings people together. Making it is simple, but a few careful steps make all the difference to the flavour. Below you will learn exactly how to prepare it. You need only a few basic ingredients, a small pot and about fifteen minutes.
Notice what the model does: it introduces the topic, explains why the task is worth doing, tells the reader what to expect, and gives an honest idea of the time and equipment needed.
Write your own opening paragraph of four to six sentences doing all four of those jobs. Do not begin any step yet.
writing.modelText: Have you ever wanted to make your classroom library a place where pupils stop and stare? An attractive display does more than tidy the shelves: it encourages readers to pick up a book they would normally walk past. In these instructions you will learn how to sort the books, make labels that communicate what each shelf holds, and build a display that persuades even the most reluctant reader. You need coloured card, marker pens, sticky tack and about one hour after school.
writing.expectedLength: One paragraph of four to six sentences
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Use the four jobs as a checklist and write one sentence for each before joining them up.
writing.extension: Rewrite your opening for a much younger reader and explain which two changes you made.

writing.title: Writing 3: Write the Full Set of Instructions
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Turn your plan and your opening paragraph into a complete procedural text.
Include all five parts in order: a clear title; your opening paragraph; a bulleted materials or equipment list; numbered steps that each begin with an imperative verb and are linked by time connectives; and a tips or warnings section.
End with one encouraging closing sentence that tells the reader they have finished.
Check your draft against this list: at least five different time connectives; at least three unit vocabulary words; at least one zero conditional sentence in your tips, such as “If you add too much sugar, the tea becomes too sweet.”
writing.modelText:
How to Make Shaah Cadays
Shaah cadays is the sweet spiced tea that unites Somali families at breakfast, and it takes about fifteen minutes.
What you will need: a small pot, water, black tea, cardamom, cinnamon, sugar, milk, a strainer.
1. First, boil the water in the pot.
2. Next, combine the tea, cardamom and cinnamon in the water.
3. After that, simmer for three minutes until a deep colour emerges.
4. Then add sugar and milk, and stir.
5. Finally, strain the tea into cups.
Tip: If you leave the pot, the milk boils over.
Enjoy your tea. You have finished!
writing.expectedLength: Full procedural text of roughly two pages
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Write the steps first and add the materials list afterwards, by collecting every object your steps mention.
writing.extension: Add a short troubleshooting section written entirely in zero conditional sentences.

writing.title: Writing 4: Peer Feedback and Final Copy
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Swap your instructions with a partner and give feedback that is kind, specific and useful.
Comment on five things. Clarity: could you actually do the task by following these steps, and which step confused you? Structure: are the title, opening, materials list, numbered steps and tips all present? Language: which imperative verbs and time connectives did you notice? Vocabulary: which unit words were used? Suggestion: name one specific improvement.
Professional recipe writers call this user testing, because the tester follows the words exactly as written. Every place your partner stops is a place to rewrite.
Use the feedback to revise your draft, then write or type your neat final copy.
writing.modelText: Strong feedback quotes the exact step that confused the reader and suggests one replacement sentence, rather than saying the writing was good.
writing.sentenceStarter: The step I could not follow was...
writing.expectedLength: One feedback sheet plus a revised final copy
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Use the five headings as sentence starters so that every comment points at something real.
writing.extension: Test your revised instructions on a second reader and record whether the confusing step disappeared.

writing.title: Writing 5: Your Memory Passage
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a passage of five to eight sentences about one personal memory that made you think, feel or learn, following the style Leo and Nora used on the Memory Wall.
Start with the moment itself rather than with the date. Include one detail that only you would remember, and one line of speech from somebody who was there.
Finish by saying what the memory taught you or why it has stayed with you.
Use at least two unit words, and read the passage aloud before you hand it in, because a memory should sound like a person talking.
writing.modelText: I still remember the moment when the bus doors closed and my mother was still on the pavement. I was six, and my hand was sticky from the mango she had given me. I did not cry, but I did not move either. The lady beside me said, "Sit down, little one, your mum will get the next bus." At the market stop I saw my mother emerge from the crowd, running. That day taught me not to hesitate when I am afraid, but to ask for help. I can still feel the mango juice on my fingers.
writing.sentenceStarter: I still remember the moment when...
writing.expectedLength: One passage of five to eight sentences
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Talk the memory through with an adult first, and write down the three details they ask about.
writing.extension: Rewrite the final two sentences so that the meaning is shown through an action rather than explained.

writing.title: Writing 6: Instructions for a Memory Wall
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine your class wants to build its own Memory Wall. Write the instructions the school would need.
Include a title, a materials list, numbered steps and at least one tip. Think about the paper, the pins, the space on the wall, how pupils will add their passages, and how long the wall will stay up.
Write for a class that has never seen a Memory Wall, so explain what it is in your opening sentence.
Add one tip written as a zero conditional, for example: “If you hang the paper too high, younger pupils cannot reach it.”
writing.modelText:
How to Build a Class Memory Wall
A Memory Wall is a place where every pupil pins up a short passage about a moment they remember.
You will need: brown paper, drawing pins, marker pens, small cards.
1. Choose an empty wall that everyone passes each day.
2. Pin the paper at pupil height.
3. Write the invitation at the top: If you remember it, write it.
4. Hand out cards and pens, and add a passage whenever a memory emerges.
5. Read one passage aloud each morning.
6. After two weeks, take the wall down and keep the cards.
Tip: If you hang the paper too high, younger pupils cannot reach it.
writing.sentenceStarter: A Memory Wall is a place where...
writing.expectedLength: One procedural text of eight to twelve steps
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with details or evidence; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Walk to a real wall in your school and note every practical problem you can see before you write.
writing.extension: Add a short paragraph explaining how the class should decide what happens to the wall at the end.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is a correct zero conditional?
quizzes.options: If you heat ice, it will melt. | If you heat ice, it melts. | If you heated ice, it melts. | If you will heat ice, it melts.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If you heat ice, it melts.
quizzes.explanation: The zero conditional puts the present simple in both halves, so no form of will and no past tense belongs there.

quizzes.question: In a zero conditional, which tense do both halves of the sentence use?
quizzes.options: Present simple | Past simple | Present perfect | Future with will
quizzes.explanation: The result is a permanent fact rather than a prediction, so both clauses stay in the present simple.

quizzes.question: Which of these sentences is a first conditional rather than a zero conditional?
quizzes.options: If it rains, the ground gets wet. | If you heat metal, it expands. | If we leave now, we will be early. | If the temperature drops below zero, water freezes.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If we leave now, we will be early.
quizzes.explanation: Only this sentence predicts one particular future occasion, and the word will in the main clause is the giveaway.

quizzes.question: Where does the comma go in a conditional sentence?
quizzes.options: After the if-clause when it comes first | Before the word if in every sentence | After the main clause when the main clause comes first | Commas are never used in conditional sentences
quizzes.correctAnswer: After the if-clause when it comes first
quizzes.explanation: The comma marks the join only when the condition is stated first; reversing the halves removes the need for it.

quizzes.question: Which of these is an imperative verb used in the bariis recipe?
quizzes.explanation: Drain is a base-form verb giving an order, while the others are an adverb, an adjective and a noun.

quizzes.question: Which of these signals the order of the steps in a procedure?
quizzes.options: measure carefully | after that | golden brown | sieve
quizzes.explanation: After that is a time connective, whereas the others name an action, a colour and a piece of equipment.

quizzes.question: According to “How to Make Bariis”, what happens if you lift the lid while the rice simmers?
quizzes.options: The rice browns and sticks to the base of the pot | The spices lose their colour | The onion begins to burn | The steam escapes and the rice stays hard
quizzes.correctAnswer: The steam escapes and the rice stays hard
quizzes.explanation: Step 7 states the consequence directly, because the trapped steam is what actually cooks the grains.

quizzes.question: In “The Memory Wall”, why does Leo feel nervous at the start?
quizzes.options: He worries that he cannot remember anything exciting | He does not like his new classroom timetable | He has forgotten his pencil case at home | He would rather draw pictures than write about himself
quizzes.correctAnswer: He worries that he cannot remember anything exciting
quizzes.explanation: Leo asks that question aloud in part 1; wanting to draw instead is Nora's reaction, not his.

quizzes.question: Nora stands at the fringe of the growing crowd. What does “fringe” mean there?
quizzes.options: The centre of it | The noise it made | The person leading it | The outer edge of it
quizzes.explanation: Fringe names a border or outer edge, which is why Nora can watch the crowd without being inside it.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word: “Do not ______ that you already know the answer without checking.”
quizzes.explanation: To assume is to treat something as true without proof, which is exactly what checking prevents.

teacherNotes.note: Model each new pattern aloud and check meaning before independent work. Give feedback on complete sentences, quoted evidence and precise vocabulary rather than on neatness. Cooking tasks are for reading and planning only; no learner handles a stove without an adult. Recording and AI tutor work happens with an adult present, and no child is left alone with the device.

Vocabulary: ask the tutor for two extra example sentences per word, then have the learner write their own and ask the tutor to check them. Useful prompts include the difference between persuade and convince, navigate used for feelings rather than directions, the noun form of enquire, the two meanings of passage, and the opposite of fade.
Grammar: ask the tutor to explain the difference between the zero and first conditional, then request five zero conditional sentences about cooking. As a challenge, ask for a mixed quiz and have the learner label each item ZC or FC.
Writing: after Writing 3, share the draft and ask the tutor whether every step could be followed by somebody who has never done the task.
Speaking: a learner working alone can ask the tutor to play the follower in the Instruction Game, or to interview them about a morning routine and summarise it back.
Always keep an adult beside the learner during tutor sessions, and treat every tutor answer as a draft to be checked against the unit texts.
